questions.question: Which organelle is the primary site of ATP production in eukaryotic cells?
questions.explanation: The mitochondrion runs oxidative phosphorylation: the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis on its inner membrane produce most cellular ATP.
questions.memoryHook: Mitos make power - the mighty mitochondria mint the energy coins.

questions.question: Sweating cools the body because water evaporating from the skin carries heat away. This cooling works because water has:
distractors: No hydrogen bonding between its molecules
A nonpolar structure that cannot store thermal energy
questions.explanation: Evaporating water molecules must break their hydrogen bonds to escape as vapor, and breaking those bonds takes energy taken from the skin. The most energetic molecules leave first, so the average kinetic energy - the temperature - of what remains on the skin falls.
questions.memoryHook: Sweat steals heat - breaking hydrogen bonds costs energy, so evaporation cools.

questions.question: The alpha-helix and the beta-pleated sheet in a protein are both held in shape mainly by:
questions.correctAnswer: Hydrogen bonds between atoms of the polypeptide backbone
distractors: Peptide bonds between adjacent amino acids
Disulfide bridges between cysteine R groups
questions.explanation: Secondary structure comes from a repeating pattern of hydrogen bonds between the carbonyl oxygen and the amide hydrogen of the backbone itself, not the R groups. Peptide bonds set the primary sequence, while disulfide bridges and ionic R-group interactions stabilize the folded tertiary shape.
questions.memoryHook: Backbone bonds build the folds - helices and sheets are hydrogen-bonded backbone patterns.

questions.question: A derived trait is present in species Q and R and absent in species P and S. Tree 1 places Q and R as sister taxa. Tree 2 places Q and S as sister taxa, with R on a separate branch. Under the principle of parsimony, which tree is preferred?
questions.correctAnswer: Tree 1, because the trait needs to evolve only once, in the common ancestor of Q and R
distractors: Tree 2, because the trait needs to evolve only once, in the common ancestor of Q and S
Both trees equally, because each tree contains the same four species
Tree 2, because sister taxa must always differ in at least one derived trait
questions.explanation: Parsimony prefers the tree requiring the fewest evolutionary changes. On Tree 1 a single origin in the shared ancestor of Q and R explains the trait in one step. On Tree 2, Q and R are not sisters, so the pattern needs at least two steps - two separate origins, or one origin plus a loss in the S lineage.
questions.memoryHook: Fewest steps wins - parsimony picks the tree with the fewest changes.

questions.question: During osmosis, water moves across a selectively permeable membrane toward the region of:
questions.explanation: Osmosis is water diffusion from a region of higher free water (lower solute) to a region of lower free water (higher solute).
questions.memoryHook: Water chases salt - water follows solute.

questions.question: Butter is a fat that stays solid at room temperature because most of its fatty acids are saturated. Saturated fatty acid tails make a fat solid mainly because they:
questions.correctAnswer: Have no carbon-carbon double bonds, so the straight tails pack tightly against each other
distractors: Have cis double bonds that bend the tails so they cannot pack closely
Contain a phosphate group that locks neighboring molecules together
Form hydrogen bonds between the carbon atoms of adjacent tails
questions.explanation: Saturated means every carbon in the tail carries the maximum number of hydrogens, so there are no double bonds and the tails stay straight. Straight tails pack closely, maximizing van der Waals interactions, so the fat is solid at room temperature. Double bonds would kink the tails and keep the fat liquid, like plant oils.
questions.memoryHook: Straight tails stack tight - saturated fats sit solid.

questions.question: A white blood cell engulfs a bacterium into a vesicle that fuses with a lysosome. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis is the engulfment of large particles like bacteria into a phagosome, which fuses with a lysosome for digestion.
questions.memoryHook: Cells eat big - phagocytosis is cell eating.

questions.question: Which element is found in every DNA nucleotide but is NOT part of any standard amino acid?
questions.explanation: Every nucleotide carries a phosphate group, so DNA always contains phosphorus. Amino acids are built from carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen, with sulfur added in cysteine and methionine - no standard amino acid contains phosphorus, which is why nitrogen and carbon fail here (they occur in both molecule types) and sulfur fails (it occurs in amino acids, not in DNA).
questions.memoryHook: P is for phosphate - phosphorus marks nucleic acids, never amino acids.

questions.question: The sodium-potassium pump moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per cycle using ATP. This is classified as:
questions.explanation: Primary active transport uses ATP directly to move solutes against their gradient. The Na+/K+ pump is the classic example.
questions.memoryHook: Pump pays ATP - primary active transport burns ATP directly.

questions.question: Which evidence BEST supports the endosymbiotic theory for mitochondria and chloroplasts?
questions.correctAnswer: They have their own circular DNA and double membranes
distractors: They are found in all eukaryotes
questions.explanation: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own small circular genomes, 70S ribosomes, and double membranes, as expected if they were once free-living prokaryotes.
questions.memoryHook: Organelles were bacteria - circular DNA hints at a bacterial past.

questions.question: A point mutation replaces a nonpolar amino acid buried in a protein's interior with a charged amino acid. The protein is still produced at normal length but no longer functions. The best explanation is that the substitution:
questions.correctAnswer: Changes how the chain folds, altering the tertiary structure and the shape of the functional region
distractors: Breaks a peptide bond at that position and splits the chain into two pieces
Changes every amino acid after that position, as a frameshift would
Deletes the gene so that no mRNA is produced
questions.explanation: Folding is driven by R-group interactions: nonpolar side chains cluster in the water-free interior, so placing a charged side chain there is energetically unfavorable and the chain refolds into a different three-dimensional shape. Because function depends on shape - for example the exact geometry of an active site - a misfolded protein fails even though its length and most of its sequence are unchanged. A substitution neither breaks bonds nor shifts the reading frame.
questions.memoryHook: Swap the side chain, wreck the fold - R groups steer folding, and shape is function.

questions.question: On a hot day, a tall tree moves water from its roots to leaves more than 30 meters above the ground with no pump. The upward pull is transmitted through the water column in the xylem mainly because water molecules stick to each other. This property of water is:
questions.correctAnswer: Cohesion, caused by hydrogen bonds between water molecules
distractors: Adhesion, caused by water molecules sticking to the leaf surface
Surface tension, caused by the skin on standing water in the roots
Root pressure, caused by osmosis pushing water up from below
questions.explanation: Transpiration evaporates water from the leaves, putting the water column under tension. Cohesion - hydrogen bonds linking each water molecule to its neighbors - keeps the column continuous so the pull is transmitted all the way down to the roots. Sticking to a different substance would be adhesion, not cohesion.
questions.memoryHook: Water holds hands with water - cohesion pulls the whole column up.

questions.question: Plants store excess glucose as starch and animals store excess glucose as glycogen. Both molecules function primarily as:
questions.correctAnswer: Energy-storage polysaccharides built from glucose monomers
distractors: Structural fibers that give plant cell walls their strength
Enzymes that speed up the digestion of sugars
Hydrophobic molecules that form cell membranes
questions.explanation: Starch and glycogen are branched polymers of glucose joined by alpha glycosidic bonds, built so glucose can be added for storage and released quickly when energy is needed. The structural glucose polymer is cellulose, a different molecule with beta bonds; storage polysaccharides are carbohydrates, not protein enzymes or membrane lipids.
questions.memoryHook: Stash the glucose - starch and glycogen are glucose savings accounts.

questions.question: What is the net ATP gain from glycolysis per glucose molecule?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis produces 4 ATP gross and consumes 2 ATP, for a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose.
questions.memoryHook: Two net from splitting sugar - glycolysis nets 2 ATP.

questions.question: Oxygen's role in aerobic respiration is to:
questions.correctAnswer: Act as the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain
distractors: Carry electrons to the Krebs cycle
questions.explanation: Oxygen accepts electrons at the end of the electron transport chain, forming water. Without it, the chain backs up.
questions.memoryHook: Oxygen ends the line - oxygen is the final electron catcher.

questions.question: Most ATP in cellular respiration is produced during:
questions.explanation: Oxidative phosphorylation (electron transport + chemiosmosis) yields about 26-28 of the ~32 ATP per glucose, the vast majority.
questions.memoryHook: The chain makes the change - oxidative phosphorylation yields the most ATP.

questions.question: In lactic acid fermentation, pyruvate is reduced to:
questions.explanation: Muscle cells reduce pyruvate to lactate, regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis can continue without oxygen.
questions.memoryHook: Muscles make lactate - no oxygen means lactate.

questions.question: The light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis occur in the:
questions.explanation: The thylakoid membranes hold photosystems II and I plus the electron transport chain that split water and make ATP and NADPH.
questions.memoryHook: Thylakoids catch light - light reactions run on thylakoid membranes.

questions.question: Triglycerides (fats) do not mix with water. This is because their three fatty acid tails are:
distractors: Negatively charged along their whole length
questions.explanation: Fatty acid tails are long hydrocarbon chains of carbon and hydrogen sharing electrons almost equally, so they carry no partial charges and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water. Water molecules bond to each other instead and exclude the tails, which is why fats separate from water and why the tails of membrane phospholipids face inward, away from water on both sides.
questions.memoryHook: Tails fear water - nonpolar hydrocarbon tails are hydrophobic.

questions.question: Which gas is released as a byproduct when water is split during photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Photolysis splits water, releasing O2 as a byproduct while providing electrons to replace those lost by photosystem II.
questions.memoryHook: Split water, free oxygen - O2 is released when water splits.

questions.question: RuBisCO is the enzyme that catalyzes:
questions.correctAnswer: Carbon fixation in the Calvin cycle
questions.explanation: RuBisCO (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase) attaches CO2 to RuBP, the first step of carbon fixation.
questions.memoryHook: RuBisCO grabs CO2 - the world's most abundant enzyme fixes carbon.

questions.question: In C4 plants, the initial CO2 fixation occurs in which cells?
questions.explanation: C4 plants first fix CO2 into a 4-carbon compound in mesophyll cells, then shuttle it to bundle-sheath cells for the Calvin cycle, minimizing photorespiration.
questions.memoryHook: Mesophyll first in C4 - C4 splits the work between two cell types.

questions.question: Chemiosmosis in mitochondria and chloroplasts both depend on:
questions.correctAnswer: A proton gradient across a membrane
distractors: Direct phosphorylation of ADP by enzymes
questions.explanation: Both use a proton (H+) gradient across a membrane to drive ATP synthase. The energy source differs (food vs light) but the mechanism is the same.
questions.memoryHook: Protons power ATP - a proton gradient drives ATP synthase in both.

questions.question: If a plant is kept in the dark, which process stops FIRST?
questions.explanation: The light reactions require photons immediately; without light they halt first, and the Calvin cycle stops soon after as ATP and NADPH run out.
questions.memoryHook: No light, no light reactions - darkness stops the light reactions first.

questions.question: Two glucose molecules join to form the disaccharide maltose, and one water molecule is released in the process. The reaction that joins monomers together this way is called:
distractors: Catabolism of a polymer by oxidation
questions.explanation: In dehydration synthesis a hydroxyl group from one monomer and a hydrogen from the other are removed as water, and the monomers bond directly - here forming a glycosidic bond. Hydrolysis is the exact reverse: it consumes a water molecule to break the bond. The same build-by-losing-water pattern assembles proteins from amino acids and nucleic acids from nucleotides.
questions.memoryHook: Lose water, link up - dehydration synthesis builds polymers.

questions.question: A G protein-coupled receptor spans the plasma membrane how many times?
questions.explanation: GPCRs are characterized by seven transmembrane alpha-helices. Ligand binding activates the associated G protein inside the cell.
questions.memoryHook: Seven spans the membrane - GPCRs weave through the membrane seven times.

questions.question: In meiosis, the two members of a homologous chromosome pair move to opposite poles of the cell during:
questions.explanation: Meiosis I is the reduction division: homologous chromosomes pair up and then separate at anaphase I, halving the chromosome number. Sister chromatids stay together through meiosis I and separate only at anaphase II.
questions.memoryHook: Partners part in phase one - homologs separate at anaphase I.

questions.question: During which mitotic phase do sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles?
questions.explanation: In anaphase, cohesin is cleaved and spindle microtubules pull sister chromatids apart toward opposite poles.
questions.memoryHook: Anaphase apart - chromatids part in anaphase.

questions.question: Cytokinesis in plant cells differs from animal cells because plant cells:
questions.correctAnswer: Form a cell plate from vesicles
distractors: Pinch inward with a cleavage furrow
questions.explanation: Plant cells build a cell plate from Golgi vesicles at the center, which becomes the new cell wall. Animal cells pinch via a cleavage furrow.
questions.memoryHook: Plants build plates - plant cytokinesis forms a cell plate.

questions.question: Checkpoints in the cell cycle primarily monitor:
questions.correctAnswer: DNA integrity and proper chromosome attachment
questions.explanation: G1, G2, and M checkpoints verify DNA is undamaged, fully replicated, and chromosomes are properly attached to the spindle.
questions.memoryHook: Checkpoints check DNA - checkpoints guard genome integrity.

questions.question: Epinephrine binds to a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) on a liver cell, starting the pathway that releases glucose from glycogen. Immediately after the receptor is activated by epinephrine, the next step in the pathway is:
questions.correctAnswer: An associated G protein releases GDP and binds GTP, becoming active
distractors: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into cyclic AMP
Protein kinase A phosphorylates enzymes that break down glycogen
The receptor enters the nucleus and switches on glucose genes
questions.explanation: The order is: ligand binds GPCR, the receptor activates a G protein (GDP is exchanged for GTP), the active G protein switches on adenylyl cyclase, adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP, and cAMP activates protein kinase A. The G protein step comes first after reception.
questions.memoryHook: Receptor wakes the G protein first - GTP on, signal on.

questions.question: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes occurs during:
questions.explanation: In prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair and exchange segments at chiasmata, creating new allele combinations.
questions.memoryHook: Cross over in prophase I - homologs swap segments in prophase I.

questions.question: In a monohybrid cross of two heterozygotes (Aa x Aa), the expected phenotypic ratio is:
questions.explanation: With complete dominance, AA and Aa (3/4) show the dominant phenotype and aa (1/4) shows recessive: a 3:1 ratio.
questions.memoryHook: Three dominant, one recessive - heterozygote cross gives 3:1.

questions.question: The genotypic ratio from Aa x Aa is:
questions.explanation: A Punnett square for Aa x Aa gives 1/4 AA, 2/4 Aa, and 1/4 aa. Counted by genotype instead of grouped by appearance, that is a 1:2:1 ratio - unlike the 3:1 phenotypic ratio, the heterozygotes are counted separately here.
questions.memoryHook: Genotypes one-two-one - Aa x Aa gives 1:2:1 genotypes.

questions.question: A dihybrid cross of two heterozygotes (AaBb x AaBb) yields what phenotypic ratio?
questions.explanation: With independent assortment and complete dominance, the classic dihybrid phenotypic ratio is 9:3:3:1.
questions.memoryHook: Nine-three-three-one - the dihybrid classic is 9:3:3:1.

questions.question: The law of independent assortment applies to genes located on:
questions.explanation: Genes on different chromosomes assort independently. Linked genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together.
questions.memoryHook: Different chromosomes, independent - independent assortment needs unlinked genes.

questions.question: A testcross is used to determine:
questions.correctAnswer: The genotype of an individual with a dominant phenotype
distractors: The mutation rate of a gene
questions.explanation: Crossing a dominant-phenotype individual with a homozygous recessive reveals whether it is AA (all dominant offspring) or Aa (1:1).
questions.memoryHook: Test the unknown - testcross reveals a hidden genotype.

questions.question: A fruit fly body cell contains 8 chromosomes (2n = 8). After a germ cell completes meiosis, how many chromosomes does each gamete contain?
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number: homologous pairs separate in meiosis I, so each product goes from diploid (2n = 8) to haploid (n = 4). Fertilization later restores the diploid number.
questions.memoryHook: Meiosis halves the deck - eight becomes four.

questions.question: ABO blood type is an example of:
questions.explanation: Three alleles (IA, IB, i) with IA and IB codominant produce four blood types.
questions.memoryHook: Three alleles, four types - ABO shows multiple alleles and codominance.

questions.question: Color blindness is X-linked recessive. A carrier mother (XBXb) and a normal father (XBY) can have:
questions.explanation: Sons get X from mother: XbY is color-blind (50% of sons). Daughters get XB from father, so none are color-blind (though 50% are carriers).
questions.memoryHook: Sons show X-linked traits - boys reveal the mother's X allele.

questions.question: Linked genes are:
questions.correctAnswer: Located close together on the same chromosome
questions.explanation: Linked genes sit near each other on the same chromosome and are usually inherited together unless crossing over separates them.
questions.memoryHook: Close genes travel together - linked genes ride the same chromosome.

questions.question: Recombination frequency between two genes is used to:
questions.correctAnswer: Map their relative positions on a chromosome
questions.explanation: One map unit (centimorgan) equals 1% recombination frequency, so crossover data builds linkage maps.
questions.memoryHook: Crossovers map genes - recombination frequency measures gene distance.

questions.question: Nondisjunction during meiosis can produce:
questions.correctAnswer: Gametes with an abnormal chromosome number
questions.explanation: Nondisjunction is the failure of chromosomes or chromatids to separate, producing aneuploid gametes (e.g., an extra chromosome 21).
questions.memoryHook: Chromosomes that won't split - nondisjunction makes aneuploid gametes.

questions.question: Down syndrome is most commonly caused by:
questions.explanation: About 95% of Down syndrome cases are trisomy 21, usually from nondisjunction in maternal meiosis.
questions.memoryHook: Three copies of 21 - trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome.

questions.question: In a pedigree, a trait appearing in every generation with affected fathers passing it to all daughters suggests:
questions.explanation: An affected father gives his X to every daughter and Y to every son, so X-linked dominant traits pass from father to all daughters.
questions.memoryHook: Father to all daughters - X-linked dominant shows that pattern.

questions.question: Epistasis occurs when:
questions.correctAnswer: One gene masks the expression of another gene
distractors: A gene is on the X chromosome
questions.explanation: In epistasis, the genotype at one locus determines whether alleles at a second locus are expressed, as in Labrador coat color.
questions.memoryHook: One gene hides another - epistasis is gene masking.

questions.question: A short DNA strand has the sequence 5'-ATGCCA-3'. Written in the 5' to 3' direction, the sequence of the complementary strand is:
questions.explanation: Base pairing is A with T and G with C, and the two strands run antiparallel. Pairing each base of 5'-ATGCCA-3' gives 3'-TACGGT-5' on the partner strand. Rewriting that partner in the standard 5' to 3' direction reverses it to 5'-TGGTAC-3'. The 5'-TACGGT-3' choice pairs the right bases but keeps the wrong direction, and uracil never appears in DNA.
questions.memoryHook: Pair it, then flip it - complement the bases and reverse for 5' to 3'.

questions.question: Three derived traits were scored in four species, and the outgroup has none of them. Trait 1 is present in species A and B only. Trait 2 is present in species A and B only. Trait 3 is present in species B and C only. Tree 1 groups (A with B) and (C with D). Tree 2 groups (A with D) and (B with C). Counting each trait gain or loss as one step, which tree is most parsimonious?
questions.correctAnswer: Tree 1, with 4 total steps, compared with 5 steps for Tree 2
distractors: Tree 2, with 4 total steps, compared with 5 steps for Tree 1
Both trees, because each requires exactly 5 total steps
Tree 1, with 3 total steps, compared with 6 steps for Tree 2
questions.explanation: On Tree 1: Trait 1 evolves once in the ancestor of A and B (1 step), Trait 2 the same (1 step), and Trait 3 must evolve separately in B and in C (2 steps) - total 4. On Tree 2: Trait 1 needs 2 steps (A and B are not grouped), Trait 2 needs 2 steps, and Trait 3 evolves once in the ancestor of B and C (1 step) - total 5. Parsimony prefers Tree 1.
questions.memoryHook: Count every change - the tree with fewer steps wins.

questions.question: DNA replication is described as semiconservative because:
questions.correctAnswer: Each new DNA molecule has one old and one new strand
distractors: Only half the genome is copied
questions.explanation: Each parental strand serves as a template, so every daughter molecule contains one original and one newly synthesized strand.
questions.memoryHook: Half old, half new - semiconservative keeps one parental strand.

questions.question: Which enzyme synthesizes the new DNA strand during replication?
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the 3' end of the growing strand. Helicase unwinds, primase lays primers, ligase joins Okazaki fragments.
questions.memoryHook: Polymerase builds - DNA polymerase synthesizes the new strand.

questions.question: The leading strand is synthesized:
distractors: In fragments away from the fork
questions.explanation: The leading strand grows continuously 5' to 3' toward the fork. The lagging strand is made as Okazaki fragments.
questions.memoryHook: Leading leads forward - the leading strand grows toward the fork.

questions.question: Cell signaling begins with the reception stage. Reception occurs when:
questions.correctAnswer: A signaling molecule (ligand) binds to a specific receptor protein on or in the target cell
distractors: A relay protein passes a phosphate group to the next protein in a cascade
The nucleus starts transcribing genes for new enzymes
The target cell divides to produce signal-producing daughter cells
questions.explanation: The three stages of signaling are reception, transduction, and response. In reception, a ligand binds a receptor - at the cell surface for water-soluble signals, or inside the cell for lipid-soluble ones. Phosphate relay belongs to transduction, and gene transcription is part of the response.
questions.memoryHook: No binding, no beginning - reception starts the signal.

questions.question: In eukaryotes, transcription occurs in the ____ and translation occurs in the ____.
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic transcription happens in the nucleus; the mRNA is exported and translated by ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
questions.memoryHook: Nucleus writes, cytoplasm builds - transcription then translation are separated.

questions.question: A codon is a sequence of how many mRNA nucleotides that specifies one amino acid?
questions.explanation: The genetic code is read in triplets; each 3-nucleotide codon specifies one amino acid (or stop).
questions.memoryHook: Three letters per word - codons are nucleotide triplets.

questions.question: tRNA molecules function to:
questions.correctAnswer: Carry amino acids to the ribosome
questions.explanation: Each tRNA has an anticodon that pairs with an mRNA codon and carries the matching amino acid to the ribosome.
questions.memoryHook: TRNA delivers cargo - tRNA brings amino acids to the ribosome.

questions.question: Introns are:
distractors: Coding sequences that remain in mRNA
questions.explanation: Introns are spliced out of pre-mRNA; exons are joined to form the mature mRNA that is translated.
questions.memoryHook: Introns exit - introns are spliced out before translation.

questions.question: A point mutation that changes one amino acid to another is called a:
questions.explanation: Missense mutations substitute one amino acid for another. Nonsense creates a stop codon; silent changes nothing; frameshift alters the reading frame.
questions.memoryHook: Missense makes a swap - missense changes one amino acid.

questions.question: In the lac operon, the repressor protein is inactivated by:
questions.explanation: Allolactose (from lactose) binds the lac repressor, releasing it from the operator so transcription can proceed.
questions.memoryHook: Allolactose unlocks - lactose's cousin frees the operon.

questions.question: Humans digest starch but cannot digest cellulose, even though both are polymers of glucose. The best explanation is that:
questions.correctAnswer: Starch uses alpha glycosidic bonds that human enzymes can break, while cellulose uses beta glycosidic bonds that human enzymes cannot break
distractors: Cellulose contains nitrogen, which human digestive enzymes cannot process
Starch uses beta glycosidic bonds and cellulose uses alpha glycosidic bonds, and human enzymes fit only the alpha form
Cellulose chains are far longer than starch chains, and human enzymes cannot process such long polymers
questions.explanation: The monomer is the same - glucose - so the difference must be in the bonds. Human amylase is shaped to hydrolyze alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds in starch, but no human enzyme fits the beta-1,4 bonds of cellulose, whose straight chains also hydrogen-bond into tough fibers. Cellulose therefore passes through as fiber unless gut microbes break it down. Both polymers contain only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
questions.memoryHook: Alpha we eat, beta we cannot - the bond angle decides dinner.

questions.question: Alternative splicing allows:
questions.correctAnswer: One gene to produce multiple different proteins
questions.explanation: By including or excluding different exons, one pre-mRNA can yield several mature mRNAs and protein variants.
questions.memoryHook: Splice many ways - alternative splicing multiplies protein options.

questions.question: In a population of rabbits in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 16% of the rabbits show the recessive phenotype for coat color. What percentage of the population is heterozygous - carriers of the recessive allele?
questions.explanation: The recessive phenotype frequency is q^2 = 0.16, so q = 0.4 and p = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6. Heterozygotes are 2pq = 2 x 0.6 x 0.4 = 0.48, or 48% of the population. (36% is p^2, the dominant homozygotes; 84% is everyone with the dominant phenotype.)
questions.memoryHook: Root of recessive gives q - 0.4 leads to 48 percent carriers.

questions.question: In gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments are separated by:
questions.explanation: All DNA is negatively charged, so fragments migrate toward the positive electrode and separate by size, with smaller fragments moving farther.
questions.memoryHook: Small runs far - gel electrophoresis sorts DNA by size.

questions.question: A plant species has a diploid number of 2n = 14, or 7 homologous chromosome pairs. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different gametes can one plant produce through independent assortment alone?
questions.explanation: Each of the 7 pairs can orient two ways at metaphase I, and the pairs assort independently, so the number of combinations is 2^n where n is the number of pairs: 2^7 = 128. (49 is 7^2, and 16,384 is 2^14 - using the diploid number instead of the number of pairs.)
questions.memoryHook: Two to the seventh - 128 gamete combos from assortment alone.

questions.question: A single hormone molecule binding to a liver cell can lead to the release of thousands of glucose molecules. A phosphorylation cascade makes this amplification possible because:
questions.correctAnswer: At each step, one activated kinase can phosphorylate and activate many copies of the next kinase, so the number of activated molecules multiplies at every level
distractors: Each phosphate group transferred in the cascade is converted into thousands of ATP molecules
The first receptor is copied thousands of times and inserted into the membrane
Each kinase produces thousands of new hormone molecules that leave the cell
questions.explanation: Kinases are enzymes, and enzymes are catalysts that are used over and over. One active kinase can activate many molecules of the next kinase before it is switched off, so a cascade multiplies the signal at every tier - this is why a tiny amount of hormone produces a massive cellular response.
questions.memoryHook: One kinase, many targets - cascades multiply the message.

questions.question: The Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium describes a population in which allele frequencies:
questions.explanation: Under Hardy-Weinberg conditions (no selection, mutation, migration, drift; random mating), allele and genotype frequencies stay constant.
questions.memoryHook: No change means equilibrium - Hardy-Weinberg is the no-evolution baseline.

questions.question: In the Hardy-Weinberg equation p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1, the term 2pq represents:
distractors: The frequency of the dominant allele
questions.explanation: In p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1, p and q are the dominant and recessive allele frequencies. The 2pq term counts both heterozygote orders (Aa and aA), so it gives the expected heterozygote frequency - for example, p = 0.8 and q = 0.2 gives 2pq = 0.32.
questions.memoryHook: Two p q is hetero - 2pq is the heterozygote frequency.

questions.question: A character table shows: lungs are present in frog, lizard, and mouse but absent in trout; an amniotic egg is present in lizard and mouse only; hair is present in mouse only. On a cladogram built from these shared derived characters, which pair of taxa is most closely related?
questions.explanation: Cladograms group taxa by shared derived characters - traits inherited from their most recent common ancestor. Lizard and mouse share two derived characters from the table, lungs and the amniotic egg, so they share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either does with the frog, which shares only lungs. Trout has none of the listed derived characters and branches off first.
questions.memoryHook: Count the shared novelties - the pair sharing the most derived traits is closest.

questions.question: Homologous structures provide evidence for evolution because they:
questions.correctAnswer: Share an underlying anatomy from a common ancestor
distractors: Perform the same function in unrelated species
questions.explanation: Homologous structures (like vertebrate forelimbs) share anatomy from common ancestry even when functions differ, unlike analogous structures.
questions.memoryHook: Same bones, shared past - homologous structures show common ancestry.

questions.question: Analogous structures, such as insect and bird wings, evolve through:
questions.explanation: Analogous structures arise independently in unrelated lineages facing similar pressures: convergent evolution.
questions.memoryHook: Similar jobs, separate origins - analogous structures converge.

questions.question: Speciation by geographic isolation is called:
questions.explanation: Allopatric speciation occurs when a geographic barrier splits a population, blocking gene flow until reproductive isolation evolves.
questions.memoryHook: Geo splits species - allopatric speciation needs a barrier.

questions.question: Which reproductive barrier acts BEFORE fertilization?
questions.explanation: Prezygotic barriers (habitat, temporal, behavioral, mechanical, gametic) prevent mating or fertilization; postzygotic barriers act after.
questions.memoryHook: Before the zygote - prezygotic barriers block fertilization.

questions.question: The fossil record showing transitional forms like Tiktaalik supports:
questions.explanation: Transitional fossils document intermediate forms between major groups, supporting evolutionary change over time.
questions.memoryHook: Fossils bridge forms - transitional fossils show descent with modification.

questions.question: Testosterone is a steroid hormone that diffuses straight through the plasma membrane of a target cell. How does testosterone trigger a response in that cell?
questions.correctAnswer: It binds a receptor inside the cell, and the hormone-receptor complex acts as a transcription factor in the nucleus, turning on specific genes
distractors: It binds a G protein-coupled receptor on the cell surface, which activates a G protein
It opens a ligand-gated ion channel in the plasma membrane, letting calcium rush in
It activates a membrane enzyme that produces the second messenger cAMP
questions.explanation: Steroid hormones are hydrophobic, so they cross the membrane and meet their receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus instead of at the surface. The hormone-receptor complex binds DNA and changes gene expression, which is why steroid responses are slower to start but longer lasting than surface-receptor responses.
questions.memoryHook: Steroids slip inside and switch genes on.

questions.question: In an F2 dihybrid cross, 160 offspring were counted: 92 showed both dominant traits, 28 showed only the first dominant trait, 31 showed only the second dominant trait, and 9 showed both recessive traits. If the two genes assort independently, the expected counts are 90, 30, 30, and 10. Using chi-square = sum of (observed - expected)^2 / expected, with a critical value of 7.82 at 3 degrees of freedom, what is the correct result?
questions.correctAnswer: Chi-square is about 0.31, which is below 7.82, so the data fit the 9:3:3:1 expectation - no evidence against independent assortment
distractors: Chi-square is about 0.31, which is below 7.82, so the hypothesis is rejected and the genes must be linked
Chi-square is about 3.1, which is above the critical value, so the hypothesis is rejected
Chi-square is about 7.82, exactly at the cutoff, so the result is borderline and inconclusive
questions.explanation: Term by term: (92-90)^2/90 = 0.04, (28-30)^2/30 = 0.13, (31-30)^2/30 = 0.03, (9-10)^2/10 = 0.10. The sum is about 0.31. Because 0.31 is far below the critical value 7.82, the deviations are consistent with chance, so the data fit the 9:3:3:1 ratio predicted by independent assortment.
questions.memoryHook: Small chi-square, good fit - 0.31 stays well under 7.82.

questions.question: Coastal cities have milder daily temperature swings than inland deserts at the same latitude. A major reason is that the nearby ocean water:
questions.correctAnswer: Absorbs large amounts of heat with only a small change in its own temperature
distractors: Has a low specific heat capacity, so it heats and cools very quickly
Contains no hydrogen bonds between its molecules
Is nonpolar, so it cannot store thermal energy
questions.explanation: Water has a high specific heat because much of the heat it absorbs goes into breaking and reforming hydrogen bonds instead of raising molecular kinetic energy. The ocean therefore warms slowly by day and releases stored heat slowly by night, buffering coastal air temperatures. A low specific heat would produce the opposite pattern - fast heating and fast cooling, like dry desert soil and rock.
questions.memoryHook: Water is a heat sponge - high specific heat smooths coastal weather.

questions.question: In a food chain, energy transfer between trophic levels is typically about:
questions.explanation: Only about 10% of energy transfers between trophic levels; the rest is lost as heat through respiration and waste.
questions.memoryHook: Ten percent passes on - trophic transfer is about 10 percent efficient.

questions.question: Primary productivity is the rate at which:
questions.correctAnswer: Producers convert light energy to chemical energy
questions.explanation: Gross primary productivity is the total photosynthetic output; net primary productivity subtracts plant respiration.
questions.memoryHook: Producers produce - primary productivity measures producer output.

questions.question: One pair of homologous chromosomes fails to separate during meiosis I - a nondisjunction event. Meiosis II then proceeds normally. The four resulting gametes will be:
questions.correctAnswer: All four abnormal: two carry an extra chromosome (n + 1) and two are missing the chromosome (n - 1)
distractors: Two normal (n), one with an extra chromosome (n + 1), and one missing the chromosome (n - 1)
All four normal (n), because the error is corrected during meiosis II
Two diploid (2n) gametes and two gametes with no chromosomes at all
questions.explanation: If homologs fail to separate in meiosis I, both homologs end up in one daughter cell and none in the other. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids normally, so the overloaded cell gives two n + 1 gametes and the empty cell gives two n - 1 gametes - all four are abnormal. (The two-normal pattern is the signature of nondisjunction in meiosis II instead.)
questions.memoryHook: A first-division slip spoils all four gametes.

questions.question: Fish that live in very cold water have cell membranes rich in phospholipids with unsaturated fatty acid tails. This helps the fish survive the cold because the unsaturated tails:
questions.correctAnswer: Contain double bonds that kink the tails, keeping the membrane fluid when cold would otherwise make it rigid
distractors: Pack tightly together, stiffening the membrane so it resists freezing damage
Carry electric charges that repel ice crystals forming outside the cell
Add extra phosphate heads that thicken and insulate the bilayer
questions.explanation: Cold makes membranes rigid as saturated tails pack and lock together. Double bonds put permanent kinks in unsaturated tails, so they cannot pack tightly and the bilayer stays fluid at low temperatures. Many organisms adjust the saturation of membrane lipids to hold fluidity roughly constant.
questions.memoryHook: Kinked tails stay loose - cold fish keep fluid membranes.

questions.question: The same gene was sequenced in four species. DNA base differences are: A-B = 2, C-D = 5, A-C = 9, B-C = 9, A-D = 10, B-D = 11. Which grouping is best supported by these molecular data?
questions.correctAnswer: A with B as closest relatives, and C with D as the other pair
distractors: A with C as closest relatives, and B with D as the other pair
All four species equally related to one another
D as the common ancestor of A, B, and C
questions.explanation: Fewer sequence differences mean less time since a common ancestor, so the smallest values identify the sister pairs: A and B differ at only 2 bases, and C and D at 5, while every cross-pair comparison is 9 or more. The data therefore support two pairs, (A, B) and (C, D). An analyzed living species is placed at a tree tip, never as the direct ancestor of other living species.
questions.memoryHook: Fewer differences, closer kin - small DNA gaps mean recent shared ancestors.

questions.question: Mimicry in which a harmless species resembles a harmful one is called:
questions.explanation: Batesian mimicry is a palatable species copying a toxic model's warning signals. Mullerian is when two harmful species resemble each other.
questions.memoryHook: Harmless copies harmful - Batesian mimicry fakes danger.

questions.question: After a meal, rising blood glucose causes the pancreas to release insulin. Insulin makes muscle and liver cells take up glucose, blood glucose falls back toward its set point, and insulin release slows. This is an example of:
questions.correctAnswer: Negative feedback, because the response counteracts the original change and restores the set point
distractors: Positive feedback, because the hormone amplifies the rise in blood glucose
A phosphorylation cascade, because insulin binds a receptor on target cells
Feedforward control, because the body prepares for the next meal in advance
questions.explanation: In negative feedback, the response reduces or reverses the stimulus: glucose rose, insulin acted to lower it, and as glucose fell the insulin signal faded. Homeostasis variables such as blood glucose, temperature, and pH are held near set points by negative feedback loops like this one.
questions.memoryHook: When the response cancels the trigger, feedback is negative.

questions.question: A cladogram of five primates shows the gibbon branching off first, then the orangutan, then the gorilla, and finally a split between the chimpanzee and the human. Which two species are sister taxa - the pair that shares the most recent common ancestor?
questions.explanation: Sister taxa branch from the same node, meaning they share a common ancestor that is more recent than any ancestor either shares with the other species. On this cladogram only the chimpanzee and the human share such a node; every other pair joins further back.
questions.memoryHook: Same node, closest kin - sister taxa share the newest ancestor.

questions.question: A keystone species is one whose removal:
questions.correctAnswer: Causes dramatic ecosystem changes disproportionate to its abundance
distractors: Has no effect on the ecosystem
questions.explanation: Keystone species (like sea otters or wolves) have outsized ecological impact relative to their numbers.
questions.memoryHook: Few in number, huge in impact - keystone species hold ecosystems together.

questions.question: Eutrophication of lakes is most often caused by:
questions.explanation: Nutrient runoff fuels algal blooms; decomposition depletes oxygen, killing fish and reducing biodiversity.
questions.memoryHook: Too many nutrients - eutrophication starts with nutrient overload.

questions.question: In many signaling pathways, a membrane receptor causes the cell to produce large amounts of cyclic AMP (cAMP) in the cytoplasm, and the cAMP then activates downstream proteins. In this role, cAMP is called a:
questions.explanation: The ligand arriving from outside is the first messenger. Small, nonprotein, water-soluble molecules like cAMP that relay the signal inside the cell - and spread it to many targets at once - are second messengers. cAMP typically works by activating protein kinase A.
questions.memoryHook: The ligand knocks outside, cAMP spreads the word inside.

questions.question: The greenhouse effect is primarily driven by gases that:
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, H2O) absorb outgoing infrared radiation, trapping heat in the atmosphere.
questions.memoryHook: Gases trap heat - greenhouse gases absorb infrared.

questions.question: A character table for five invertebrates shows: segmented body - earthworm, spider, ant, butterfly; jointed legs - spider, ant, butterfly; six legs - ant, butterfly; wings - butterfly only. The snail has none of these traits. Which trait is a shared derived character (synapomorphy) that unites the ant and the butterfly in a clade that excludes the spider?
questions.explanation: A synapomorphy must be shared by the clade members, newly evolved in their common ancestor, and absent in the groups being excluded. Six legs is shared by ant and butterfly but absent in the spider. Jointed legs also occur in the spider, segmented body also occurs in the earthworm, and wings are found only in the butterfly, so none of those can define the ant-butterfly clade.
questions.memoryHook: Six legs make the team - ant and butterfly share the trait.

questions.question: In mark-recapture studies, population size is estimated using the formula:
questions.correctAnswer: N = (marked in first sample x total in second sample) / recaptured marked
questions.explanation: The Lincoln-Petersen estimator assumes marked and unmarked animals mix randomly: N = (M x C) / R.
questions.memoryHook: Mark, release, recapture - mark-recapture estimates population size.

questions.question: A plant cell is placed in an open container at 300 K. The cell's pressure potential (PsiP) is +4.0 bars, and its cytoplasm contains a 0.20 mol/L solution of a solute that does not ionize (i = 1). Using PsiS = -iCRT, where R = 0.0831 L bars/(mol K), and Psi = PsiP + PsiS, what is the cell's total water potential?
questions.explanation: First the solute potential: PsiS = -(1)(0.20)(0.0831)(300) = -4.99, about -5.0 bars. Then add the pressure potential: Psi = PsiP + PsiS = +4.0 + (-5.0) = -1.0 bars. (-5.0 bars is the solute potential alone, before the pressure potential is added.) Water always moves toward the lower, more negative, water potential.
questions.memoryHook: Pressure pushes back - plus 4 meets minus 5 for minus 1.

questions.question: A chi-square test in genetics is used to determine whether:
questions.correctAnswer: Observed ratios differ significantly from expected ratios
questions.explanation: Chi-square compares observed offspring counts to expected Mendelian ratios; a large value suggests the hypothesis should be rejected.
questions.memoryHook: Chi-square checks fit - chi-square tests observed vs expected.

questions.question: A cladogram of five vertebrates shows the lamprey branching off first, then the trout, then the frog, with lizard and mouse as sister taxa. Which taxon serves as the outgroup in this cladogram?
questions.explanation: The outgroup is the lineage that diverged before the common ancestor of all the other taxa in the tree - here the lamprey, a jawless fish lacking the shared derived characters (such as jaws) that unite the trout, frog, lizard, and mouse as the ingroup. Comparing the ingroup against the outgroup tells researchers which character states are ancestral and which are derived.
questions.memoryHook: First branch out - the earliest diverging lineage is the outgroup.

questions.question: Enzyme activity typically increases with temperature up to an optimum because:
questions.correctAnswer: Higher kinetic energy increases successful collisions
questions.explanation: Heat raises molecular motion and collision frequency until high temperatures denature the enzyme.
questions.memoryHook: Heat speeds collisions - temperature raises reaction rate until denaturation.

questions.question: A competitive inhibitor affects an enzyme by:
questions.correctAnswer: Binding the active site and blocking substrate
questions.explanation: Competitive inhibitors mimic the substrate and occupy the active site; raising substrate concentration can overcome them.
questions.memoryHook: Competes for the site - competitive inhibitors block the active site.

questions.question: Feedback inhibition in metabolic pathways usually involves:
questions.correctAnswer: The end product inhibiting an early enzyme
questions.explanation: End-product inhibition shuts down the pathway's first committed step when enough product accumulates, conserving resources.
questions.memoryHook: Product stops production - feedback inhibition uses the end product as a brake.

questions.question: PCR (polymerase chain reaction) is used to:
questions.explanation: PCR cycles of denaturation, annealing, and extension exponentially copy a target DNA region using primers and Taq polymerase.
questions.memoryHook: PCR photocopies DNA - PCR amplifies target DNA sequences.

questions.question: Heating an egg white denatures its proteins: the white turns solid and opaque as the protein molecules unfold. Denaturation by heat disrupts the forces holding the folded shape, but it does NOT break the protein's:
questions.correctAnswer: Primary structure - the amino acid sequence held together by peptide bonds
distractors: Hydrogen bonds that hold alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets in shape
Hydrophobic interactions that tuck nonpolar side chains into the interior
Ionic attractions between charged side chains on the folded surface
questions.explanation: Heat shakes apart the weak interactions - hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and ionic attractions - that maintain secondary and tertiary structure, so the protein unfolds and loses function. The primary structure is a chain of covalent peptide bonds, and ordinary heating does not hydrolyze them, so the amino acid sequence stays intact.
questions.memoryHook: Heat unravels the fold, not the chain - the sequence survives.

questions.question: Which molecule carries electrons from glycolysis and the Krebs cycle to the electron transport chain?
questions.explanation: NADH (and FADH2) shuttle high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain, where their energy pumps protons.
questions.memoryHook: NADH hauls electrons - NADH delivers electrons to the chain.

questions.question: C3 plants close stomata on hot days to conserve water, which causes:
questions.correctAnswer: Reduced CO2 intake and increased photorespiration
questions.explanation: Closed stomata limit CO2 entry, so RuBisCO fixes O2 instead, wasting energy through photorespiration.
questions.memoryHook: Closed pores starve carbon - closed stomata trigger photorespiration.

questions.question: The central dogma of molecular biology states that information flows:
questions.explanation: The central dogma: DNA is transcribed to RNA, which is translated to protein (with reverse transcription as a known exception).
questions.memoryHook: DNA writes RNA builds protein - the central dogma flows DNA to RNA to protein.
